summary:
Our project acts as an interactive Earth system detective tool designed to uncover, visualize, and validate long-term environmental changes using open NASA Earth science data. Because Earth’s subsystems constantly interact and shift differently across regions, our solution simplifies the process of turning raw satellite and model measurements into clear, actionable insights.
Methodology & Key Features
• Variable & Region Selection. Users can select specific Earth science indicators (such as [insert your variable, e.g., land surface temperature / sea ice extent / precipitation]) and isolate localized geographic regions where meaningful environmental shifts occur.
• Time-Series Visualization. The platform generates clean, multi-year time-series visualizations that make complex historical fluctuations easy to observe at a glance.
• Statistical Trend Validation. Beyond visual charts, our tool calculates the exact rate of change and applies statistical significance testing (using [insert your method, e.g., Mann-Kendall test / t-test / confidence intervals]) to confirm whether observed patterns represent true environmental trends rather than random noise.
Impact
By answering what is changing, where it is happening, how fast it is shifting, and whether it is statistically significant, our project empowers researchers, decision-makers, and everyday citizens to better understand our changing planet.
details: Earth System Trend Detective is a guided tool that helps students and curious members of the public find out whether an Earth system variable is really changing in their region, and whether that change is statistically significant. The user picks a variable (with a plain-language definition), uploads a monthly time series for their region, and gets a chart with the seasonal cycle removed, the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence range, and a plain-language verdict. Under the hood, the tool uses monthly anomalies, the Theil-Sen slope, the Mann-Kendall test, and the Hamed-Rao correction for autocorrelation, so results are not overstated. As a case study, we analysed NASA GPM IMERG monthly precipitation (2002-2019) for a Karachi, Pakistan region from NASA Giovanni. The tool found no statistically significant trend (about +0.0002 mm/hr per decade, 95% range -0.0022 to +0.0029, corrected p = 0.79), and annual-mean and monsoon-season re-analyses agreed. We also report the limitations: a short 18-year record, many near-zero months in a dry region, and linear-only trend testing. The app is built with Python, SciPy, pandas and Streamlit, and is validated with automated tests on synthetic data with known trends.
